agent_trace.summary: On a chest X-ray, lung hyperinflation is assessed by looking for increased lung volume, low or flattened diaphragms, and a relatively narrow, elongated cardiac silhouette. The retrieved similar cases mainly show that this is a standard chest radiograph context; the current question specifically asks about an air-trapping pattern rather than opacity. Hyperinflation can be seen with obstructive airway disease, but interpretation should rely on the full radiographic appearance and clinical context.

key_facts: Hyperinflated lungs appear larger than expected, often with increased radiolucency and expanded lung fields.
Flattening or depression of the diaphragms is a classic clue to hyperinflation.
An increased retrosternal air space on the lateral view also supports hyperinflation.
The heart may appear narrow or vertically oriented due to lung overexpansion.
Normal inspiratory effort can mimic mild hyperinflation, so technique matters.
